In Chromium, a native button fires
on key down for Enter and on key up for Space, and this script copies that timing. It still has no
support and no form behavior, and every team that fakes a button writes its own slightly different copy.
Links have the same trap in reverse. MDN points out that people expect a button to respond to Space or Enter but a link only to Enter, so a link dressed up with
needs a Space handler too. Choose the element by what it does: a button performs an action on the page, and a link takes the user somewhere.

MDN quotes the first rule of ARIA use: "If you can use a native HTML element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible, then do so." WCAG 2.2 points the same way. Its Understanding document for 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A) notes that standard HTML controls already meet the criterion when used according to the specification; custom controls need extra work. And a control that can't be operated from the keyboard fails 2.1.1 Keyboard, also Level A.
For the checkout, the fix is one element:

content.text: Most fake buttons exist because a native button looks like a native button. A few declarations remove that:
font: inherit; color: inherit; background: none; border: none; padding: 0;
